question: A 9-month-old boy is confirmed to have a first febrile UTI. He responds well to IV antibiotics within 48 hours. Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?

answers.text: DMSA scan within 4–6 months to detect renal scarring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DMSA is the gold standard for scarring but is not the first-line investigation. Ultrasound is performed first to assess anatomy.

answers.text: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) within 6 weeks to exclude vesicoureteric reflux

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MCUG is indicated in selected cases (e.g., abnormal ultrasound, recurrent UTI, high-grade reflux suspicion) but is not the universal first investigation. Renal ultrasound comes first.

answers.text: Renal ultrasound to assess anatomy, hydronephrosis, and upper tract dilatation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ultrasound is the first-line, radiation-free investigation for all children after febrile UTI. It answers 'is the anatomy normal?' — detecting hydronephrosis, duplex systems, or PUJ obstruction.

answers.text: CT urogram with contrast to fully characterise the renal tract

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT urogram is not indicated in a child with a first febrile UTI. The radiation dose is unacceptable when ultrasound (and selectively MCUG/DMSA) provides the required information.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the three-tool strategy: USG (anatomy) → MCUG if reflux suspected → DMSA for scarring. They are complementary, not interchangeable. USG is always the starting point.
Correct. Ultrasound first — it answers the anatomy question without radiation and guides whether further imaging (MCUG, DMSA) is warranted.
